analysis.one_liner: Requires delivery apps to show full prices and fees upfront and bans fees based on personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in April 2026, would force delivery apps to display all fees clearly and stop setting fees using personal data, but it has no cosponsors and has not moved past the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The PRICE Act would set pricing rules for third-party delivery platforms like DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, and Instacart. Apps would have to show the restaurant's own price and any delivery fee as you shop, display a running total of everything you will be charged, and explain each fee before you pay. It would also bar platforms from setting fees based on data about you — like your past purchases or how price-sensitive the app thinks you are — and from building fees on secret deals with restaurants. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who orders food, groceries, or goods through delivery apps. They would see the true cost of an order as they build it, instead of discovering service fees, delivery fees, and other charges at checkout. The ban on personalized pricing would also protect people the algorithms currently charge more, and the ban on arrangement-based fees would make prices comparable across restaurants. Restaurants could also benefit, since customers would see the menu price the restaurant actually charges rather than a marked-up app price.

how_it_helps.text: Delivery platforms would have to show the restaurant's own price for each item and any delivery fee the moment you select the item, and display a running total — items, taxes, and fees — throughout the order, so there are no surprise charges at checkout.

Delivery fees could only be figured from the order's price and delivery factors like distance, and could not change once you start your order. Fees could not be set using proxies for your personal characteristics, such as inferred price sensitivity, past buying behavior, or willingness to pay — in other words, no charging you more because the app's data says you'll tolerate it.

Before payment, the app must explain every fee in a clear and non-misleading way — what it is for, how much it is, and whether it is refundable — and fees could not be based on behind-the-scenes deals between the platform and the restaurant.

The rules would be enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission as an unfair or deceptive practice, and by state attorneys general, who could sue on behalf of residents to stop violations and win restitution or damages for customers.

analysis.who_pays: Third-party delivery platforms. They would carry the cost of changing their apps and pricing systems, would lose the ability to earn more from customers their data shows will pay more, and would face FTC enforcement and state lawsuits for violations. Some of that cost could show up as somewhat higher base fees, though the bill requires those fees to be disclosed.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires honesty about fees but does not cap them. A platform could still charge a very large delivery fee as long as it is disclosed upfront and calculated from the order price and distance, so the total cost of delivery could stay just as high.

Platforms would need to rebuild pricing and checkout systems to meet the display and fee-methodology rules within 90 days of enactment, on top of FTC rulemaking, and violators face FTC penalties and state attorney general lawsuits — real compliance costs for the industry.

The rule that a fee methodology is fixed once you pick a restaurant, and based only on order price and delivery distance, could limit features some customers like, such as promotions or price breaks that vary during an order, though the bill does allow tips to work as before.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For customers, the upside is real but moderate: honest, complete pricing on delivery orders and a prohibition on charging people more based on their personal data. The compliance burden falls on large platforms that already price orders digitally, so the cost is modest for them. The biggest limitation is that the bill targets how fees are shown and calculated, not how large they are — so it fixes surprise fees, not necessarily expensive delivery.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no committee action so far.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján introduced the PRICE Act in the Senate on April 27, 2026.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which is where the bill now sits.
No senator has signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee has held no markup, hearing, or vote on the bill in the record so far.
The bill text lays out pricing, disclosure, and anti-personalized-pricing rules for delivery platforms, with FTC and state attorney general enforcement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major delivery platforms are better off so far: none of the bill's disclosure and pricing restrictions apply, and fee and personalized-pricing practices continue as they are.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Luján
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: There are no cosponsors and no votes yet, so no partisan pattern has formed around the bill.

industries.industry: Third-party delivery platforms (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Instacart)
industries.note: These apps make much of their money from fees stacked on top of restaurant prices and from pricing that varies with what their data says a customer will pay. The bill would force fee transparency, ban data-driven and deal-based fee setting, and expose them to FTC and state enforcement.

Customers would see the price the restaurant itself charges, not a marked-up app price, which could make ordering through apps more attractive and keep platforms' cut of restaurant prices from feeding opaque fees. Restaurants lose nothing under the bill's rules, which apply to the platforms.

Businesses that supply personalized-pricing tools — models built on purchase history and inferred willingness to pay — would lose a use case, since the bill bans fee methods that rely on proxies for user characteristics.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the early profile of most private member's bills: one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and a referral to the Senate Commerce Committee with no scheduled hearing or markup. Unless it attracts cosponsors and committee attention — or is folded into a larger package such as a junk-fee or Federal Trade Commission reauthorization bill — it is likely to sit in committee and expire when this Congress ends in January 2027.
